ARR.tip: Your total subscription revenue if every current customer stayed for a full year. It's the number VCs care about most for SaaS companies.

MRR.tip: The subscription revenue you can count on each month. ARR is just this times 12.

cash_on_hand.tip: How much money you currently have. You use this to pay salaries, hosting, and all other costs.

quarterly_revenue.tip: The money your company earns in one quarter. If this is higher than money out, your cash grows.

quarterly_burn.tip: Total spending in one quarter: team salaries, hosting/infrastructure, office, and other operating costs.

burn_rate.tip: Your total costs per quarter. If you're spending more than you earn, you're 'burning' through your savings. Every startup founder checks this obsessively.

runway.short: How long until you run out of money
runway.tip: Cash divided by burn rate. If you have $300K and burn $100K per quarter, you have 3 quarters of runway. When this hits zero, it's game over — literally.

churn_rate.tip: The percentage of your users who stop using your product each quarter. High churn means your product isn't sticky enough — people try it and leave.

tech_debt.short: Shortcuts that slow you down later
tech_debt.tip: When you ship code fast and cut corners, it works now but makes everything harder later. Like credit card debt — easy to accumulate, painful to pay off. Assign engineers to Tech Debt to reduce it.

dau.tip: How many people actually use your product each day. A big user count with low DAU means people signed up but don't come back — that's a problem.

ux_score.short: How good your product feels to use
ux_score.tip: User experience quality. Higher UX means better conversion and retention — people stick around when the product feels good. Assign engineers to R&D to improve this.

stability.tip: Server uptime and reliability. Low stability means outages, which means users leave. Assign engineers to Infrastructure to improve this.

morale.short: How your team feels about working here
morale.tip: Happy employees work better and stay longer. Overwork, low pay, and chaos tank morale. Below 60 morale, employees start thinking about quitting.

stress.tip: Builds up from being assigned to work. High stress eats into morale over time. Employees recover stress gradually each quarter, but piling it on leads to burnout.

skill.short: How good someone is at their job
skill.tip: A higher skill means more and better output each quarter. Employees with high growth potential improve their skill over time if they're assigned to work.

equity.tip: How much of the company you own. You start at 100%. Every time you raise money from investors, you give up some equity in exchange for cash. Less equity means less payout if you sell.

dilution.short: Losing ownership when you raise money
dilution.tip: When investors put money in, they get a percentage of the company. Your ownership goes down — that's dilution. A $2M raise at a $10M valuation means giving up 20%.

valuation.short: What investors think your company is worth
valuation.tip: Not real money — it's a negotiated number. A higher valuation means you give up less equity for the same amount of cash. VCs and founders haggle over this.

seed_round.tip: The first major investment in your company, usually $500K–$3M. Comes from angel investors or early-stage VCs. Used to build the product and find initial customers.

series_a.tip: A bigger round, usually $5M–$15M. Investors want to see product-market fit — real users, real revenue, real growth. This is where many startups fail to raise.

product_market_fit.short: People actually want what you built
product_market_fit.tip: The magic moment when your product meets real demand. Users grow organically, retention is strong, and people recommend it without being asked. Every startup is searching for this.

cac.tip: How much you spend to get one new customer. Marketing spend divided by new customers. If CAC is higher than what a customer pays you, you're losing money on every user.

ltv.tip: Total revenue you'll earn from one customer over their entire time using your product. The golden rule: LTV needs to be at least 3x your CAC, or the math doesn't work.

gmv.tip: Total value of transactions on your marketplace. If 1,000 items sell for $50 each, your GMV is $50K. Your actual revenue is the take rate — the small percentage you keep from each sale.

take_rate.tip: The percentage a marketplace keeps from each sale. Uber takes ~25%, Airbnb takes ~14%, the App Store takes 30%. Higher take rate means more revenue but pushes sellers to competitors.

saas.tip: Software you pay for monthly or yearly instead of buying once. Think Slack, Notion, Dropbox. Predictable recurring revenue makes this the most popular startup model.

b2b.tip: Your customers are other companies, not regular people. B2B deals are bigger but take longer to close. One enterprise contract can be worth thousands of consumer subscriptions.

ipo.tip: When a private company sells shares to the public for the first time. The ultimate exit — your company is now traded on the stock market. Requires massive revenue and scale.

pivot.short: Changing direction when something isn't working
pivot.tip: Startups pivot when their original idea isn't gaining traction. Slack started as a gaming company. Instagram started as a check-in app. Sometimes the pivot is the company.

bootstrapping.tip: Growing your company using only revenue and personal savings — no VC money. Full control, no dilution, but slower growth and every dollar matters.

board_seat.short: An investor's seat at the decision table
board_seat.tip: When VCs invest, they often get a seat on your board of directors. The board can influence major decisions — and if things go badly, they can replace you as CEO.

term_sheet.tip: A document outlining the terms of an investment — how much money, at what valuation, what control they get. It's not legally binding, but it's the framework for the final deal.

assign_features.tip: Engineers assigned to Features work on shipping new functionality. More features attract more users. Feature quality depends on engineer skill — high-skill engineers ship better work.

assign_bugs.tip: Engineers assigned to Bug Fixes reduce your bug count. Fewer bugs means less user churn. Bugs accumulate naturally — especially when tech debt is high.

assign_tech_debt.tip: Tech debt builds up when you ship fast and cut corners. High tech debt slows down ALL work and generates more bugs. Assign engineers here to pay it down.

assign_infra.tip: Infrastructure work keeps your servers running. Low stability causes outages, which drives users away. Essential as your user base grows.

assign_rnd.tip: R&D improves your product's user experience score. Better UX means users enjoy your product more, stay longer, and recommend it to others.

unicorn.short: A startup valued at $1 Billion or more
unicorn.tip: The mythical creature of the startup world. Reaching a $1B valuation puts you in rare company — fewer than 1% of startups ever get here. One of the ways to win the game.

acqui_hire.short: Getting bought for your team, not your product
acqui_hire.tip: When a bigger company buys your startup mainly to hire your engineering team. The product usually gets shut down. It's a soft landing — not a home run, but not a failure either.

profit_streak.tip: The number of quarters in a row where your revenue exceeded your burn rate. Hit 4 consecutive profitable quarters after Year 3 and you've built a sustainable business — that's a win.

founder_background.tip: Your chosen background gives stat bonuses that affect gameplay. Engineers build better products. Finance founders stretch cash further. Recruiters keep teams happier. Hustlers grow users faster.

founder_energy.short: How close you are to burning out
founder_energy.tip: Running a startup takes a personal toll. Low cash, quitting employees, and working alone drain your energy. Profitable quarters and a happy team help you recharge. Hit zero and you burn out — game over.

board_patience.short: How happy your investors are with your progress
board_patience.tip: After raising VC money, your board expects growth. Miss targets for too long and they'll replace you as CEO. Grow users, revenue, or ship features to keep them satisfied. Bootstrapped companies don't have this problem.

economy_state.tip: The broader economy shifts every few quarters. Bull markets make fundraising easier and users grow faster. Bear markets mean tighter budgets, slower growth, and cautious investors. You can't control it — just adapt.

company_valuation.short: What your company is estimated to be worth
company_valuation.tip: Valuation updates each quarter based on revenue, users, growth rate, team size, and market conditions. SaaS companies are valued on revenue multiples. Consumer companies on per-user value. Fundraising sets a floor.

mrr.short: How much subscription revenue comes in each month
mrr.tip: MRR is the heartbeat of a SaaS business. It's your quarterly revenue divided by 3. Investors love predictable, recurring revenue — it's the main driver of SaaS valuations.

dau_mau.short: Daily active users as a percentage of monthly users
dau_mau.tip: Measures how often users come back. A 50%+ ratio means users open the app almost every day — that's exceptional. Below 20% means most users are dormant. Social media apps typically aim for 40%+.

gmv.short: Total value of goods sold through your marketplace
gmv.tip: GMV is the total transaction volume — not your revenue. Your actual revenue is the cut you take (the 'take rate'). A marketplace with $1M GMV and a 10% take rate earns $100K.

api_calls.short: How many times developers hit your API per quarter
api_calls.tip: For developer tools, API calls measure real usage. More calls mean deeper integration into customers' tech stacks, making them less likely to switch. Usage-based pricing ties revenue directly to this metric.

feature_tree.short: The set of features you can build, specific to your company type
feature_tree.tip: Each company type has its own feature tree with 10 features. Some require prerequisites — for example, you need a User Dashboard before you can build Analytics. Each feature has a build cost and gameplay effects like reduced churn or increased revenue.
